slides.title:
BOT TEAMS.
REAL WORK.
slides.body: People and their AIs, connected to finish the work together.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Turn separate assistants into a working team.
bullets: One network for conversations, context and action.
A workspace, a directory and a market for useful bots.

expanded.title: Turn separate assistants into a working team
body: Businesses already use multiple assistants, apps and communication channels. BotBar brings them into a shared workflow, so people can ask for a result instead of carrying every message and file between systems.
The business combines everyday access through the keyboard, collaboration through BotBoard, and a network where people can reach, discover and buy bot services.

slides.sourceLabel: Product direction and investment opportunity | November 2026

slides.title:
THE HANDOFF
IS THE BOTTLENECK.
slides.body: A conversation can move instantly. The work behind it often starts over.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: The customer pays for the gaps between systems.
bullets: Customer history lives in one place.
The answer or action lives somewhere else.
A person has to connect the pieces.

expanded.title: The customer pays for the gaps between systems
body: A sales representative may need a quote, a customer conversation and a calendar before offering the next step. A service agent may need another specialist without making the customer repeat the story.
The opportunity is to reduce that coordination burden: keep the right context with the task and make the next authorized action easier to complete.

rows.label: Buyer
rows.detail: Contact-center leaders, service-business owners and teams managing customer follow-up.

rows.label: Cost of the problem
rows.detail: Repeated briefings, dropped follow-ups, time spent copying information and handoffs without a clear owner.

slides.title:
BOTS THAT
WORK TOGETHER.
slides.body: A connected team can carry the context, coordinate the task and return a useful result.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Keep the work connected across channels.
bullets: Messages, email and files.
Shared voice and background coordination.
Tools and app actions with people in control.

expanded.title: Keep the work connected across channels
body: Email is one way to exchange information. The broader product brings conversations, files, instructions and supported actions into the same team workflow.

One assistant can gather an answer, another can use it in an authorized task, and a person can guide the discussion. The goal is continuity from request to result, including while the team is speaking.

rows.label: Kloudy MCP
rows.detail: The connection for bot messages, data and tool coordination.

rows.label: BotBar + Keyboard
rows.detail: The interaction surface for supported app work and information exchange.

rows.label: BotBoard
rows.detail: The shared place to see the team, combine work areas and continue the task.

slides.sourceLabel: Product scope. Availability varies by connected system and supported workflow.

slides.title:
FOLLOW UP.
FOLLOW THROUGH.
slides.body: Start with call centers and service businesses that already pay to turn customer interest into action.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Sell a recurring business job with a clear owner.
bullets: Recover eligible leads and unfinished quotes.
Help a representative resolve questions.
Coordinate a booking or informed handoff.

expanded.title: Sell a recurring business job with a clear owner
body: The first offer is a focused workflow for a team that already has customers, approved outreach and a reason to follow up. The buyer is the person responsible for customer response, sales operations or service delivery.
A paid pilot establishes whether the team can complete the job reliably. Expansion follows useful results and repeat use, rather than asking a business to replace every system at once.

rows.label: Customer value
rows.detail: Less re-briefing and manual coordination; a more complete next step for the customer.

rows.label: Revenue route
rows.detail: Paid team services, recurring workflow subscriptions and metered optional communication services.

slides.title:
FROM OUTREACH
TO OUTCOME.
slides.body: “Follow up on approved quotes, answer questions and help interested customers book.”
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Each participant contributes to the same outcome.
bullets: Prepare the relevant history and instructions.
Let the right people and bots contribute.
Return the booking, handoff or next step.

expanded.title: Each participant contributes to the same outcome
body: The task starts with the customer’s approved records and instructions. A specialist can answer a question or check a supported tool while the lead participant keeps the conversation moving.
The workflow ends with a returned result and an updated business record. That makes the product useful for sales follow-up, service coordination and collaboration between client teams.

rows.label: Prepare
rows.detail: Gather the permitted context and assign the task.

rows.label: Converse
rows.detail: Use voice, messages or email as appropriate; share relevant files and answers.

rows.label: Complete
rows.detail: Make the supported booking or handoff and record the result.

rows.label: Continue
rows.detail: Keep the next step available to the authorized team.

slides.sourceLabel: Designed customer workflow; connected actions follow the customer’s permissions.

slides.title:
THE TEAM,
AT YOUR FINGERTIPS.
slides.body: Put useful AI work where people already type, speak and interact with their screens.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Own an everyday point of access.
bullets: Reach a bot without rebuilding the workflow.
Move information across supported app interactions.
Discover useful services through visible keys.

expanded.title: Own an everyday point of access
body: The keyboard gives BotBar a recurring point of contact with the user. Supported screen interactions connect the request to useful work in an app, with the user’s permissions.

That distribution surface also creates commercial inventory: relevant partner keys, sponsored placements and paths from a useful action to a bot’s store listing. The keyboard remains an entry point to the broader network.

rows.label: For users
rows.detail: Familiar typing and voice controls, with their bot team close at hand.

rows.label: For partners
rows.detail: A visible, contextual route to discovery at the moment a customer needs help.

slides.sourceLabel: Product design vision. Screen actions depend on supported OS capabilities and user permissions.

slides.title:
YOUR TEAM.
ON ONE BOARD.
slides.body: A shared workspace for the people, bots, apps and projects behind the task.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Make collaboration understandable and usable.
bullets: Open, expand, arrange and combine work areas.
See the participants and their contributions.
Return to a connected project across sessions.

expanded.title: Make collaboration understandable and usable
body: BotBoard is the place where the connections become a coherent experience. Users can see which assistants are involved, what they are discussing and the work they are producing.
Combining work areas must connect the actual task and participants. The intended result is a workspace someone can use independently, with continuity between the conversation and its outcome.

rows.label: Commercial role
rows.detail: A home for ongoing team work and paid collaboration services.

rows.label: Experience
rows.detail: A clean, futuristic environment built around real activity and meaningful controls.

slides.sourceLabel: Product design vision; illustrated appearance is not a runtime acceptance screenshot.

slides.title:
YOUR HANDLE.
YOUR BOT TEAM.
slides.body: People own their handles. BotBar operates the directory, vetting and marketplace around them.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: An address people can build a relationship around.
bullets: A memorable identity for a bot or team.
Vetted admission and clear ownership.
Approved contacts and sharing instructions.

expanded.title: An address people can build a relationship around
body: A handle lets someone reach a person’s bot team again without rediscovering the provider, device or conversation. The owner controls which bots belong to the handle and which contacts can share information.

BotBar’s role is to operate that network: registration, bot-admission standards, discovery and the store. Identity and bot vetting support trust; they do not give an unknown contact access to private data.

rows.label: Owners
rows.detail: Claim and manage their identity, bots, teams and contact relationships.

rows.label: Network operator
rows.detail: Runs the directory, admission process and marketplace rules.

rows.label: Creators
rows.detail: Can register, distribute and sell useful bots through the same network.

slides.sourceLabel: Network design and ownership model. Vetting scope and handle terms are part of launch readiness.

slides.title:
MEET WHERE
WORK HAPPENS.
slides.body: Carry the same team and task across shared calls, messages, email and business meetings.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Let the channel serve the job.
bullets: Human + bot conversations in BotBar and BotBoard.
Zoom and Microsoft Teams integration goals.
Bandwidth as an option for calls, SMS and conferencing.

expanded.title: Let the channel serve the job
body: A person can participate in the voice conversation while assistants exchange context and coordinate useful work. Email, files and messages remain available when a task does not need another spoken turn.

Meeting and telephone options extend that experience into the environments customers already use. The business can offer paid communication services without making every internal bot message a telephone or email transaction.

slides.sourceLabel: Integration goals; availability depends on supported provider routes. Third-party names do not imply partnership.

slides.title:
A SMALL SHARE.
A REAL BUSINESS.
slides.body: Annual revenue opportunity at 0.25% of each reported market.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Start with budgets already committed to customer work.

expanded.title: Start with budgets already committed to customer work
body: Cloud contact centers and sales software are existing spending categories. BotBar’s entry is a focused coordination workflow, sold to buyers responsible for follow-up, service and team productivity.

Using the published annual revenue bases, a 0.25% share corresponds to $21 million in contact centers or $64.25 million in CRM sales software. The opportunity is to earn a small share of established spending through useful customer workflows.

rows.label: How revenue is earned
rows.detail: Team services, subscriptions and supported workflow or communication usage.

rows.label: What the calculation means
rows.detail: Market size × 0.0025. Conditional annual revenue, not profit, achieved share or a forecast. These overlapping markets are not added together.

slides.sourceLabel: USD. Reported market estimates × 0.25%; conditional revenue, not a forecast. Markets are not additive.

slides.title:
MORE CHANNELS.
MORE OPPORTUNITY.
slides.body: Communication services and paid discovery expand the business beyond subscriptions.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Two additional ways to earn from useful adoption.

expanded.title: Two additional ways to earn from useful adoption
body: Communication services address businesses paying to connect conversations and workflows. Advertising and sponsorship address suppliers paying for relevant discovery. These are different buyers and different revenue mechanisms.

At 0.25% of the reported annual market revenue, programmable communications represents $37.25 million; U.S. display advertising represents $204 million. The advertising category is a broad opportunity reference, not a measured bot-keyboard market.

rows.label: Communication services
rows.detail: Paid messaging, voice and white-label offers for businesses using the network.

rows.label: Discovery
rows.detail: Sponsored keyboard keys and promoted store listings, sold on relevance and measurable engagement.

rows.label: Market boundaries
rows.detail: Independent opportunities with different scopes. Do not add these figures to the previous page or treat them as a minimum return.

slides.sourceLabel: USD. 0.25% share calculation, not a forecast. Broad adjacent markets; not BotBar’s measured serviceable market.

slides.title:
LIGHTWEIGHT
BY DESIGN.
slides.body: Direct bot-to-bot traffic does not need a paid SMS or email for every exchange.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Low transport cost can support several revenue streams.
bullets: Keep routine coordination on the digital network.
Use models, voice and phone channels when valuable.
Match variable services to paid usage.

expanded.title: Low transport cost can support several revenue streams
body: The economic advantage is separating inexpensive information transport from paid intelligence and telephone delivery. Routine data and signals can move without requiring a new model answer or carrier transaction each time.

A published cloud reference illustrates the scale: AWS lists standard queue requests at $0.40 per million in its cost example, equivalent to $0.0000004 per request. That is a component reference, not BotBar’s measured all-in cost or a one-request-per-message assumption.

Twilio’s U.S. SMS starts at $0.0083 per segment plus carrier fees. AgentMail’s Developer plan lists $20 per month for 10,000 emails and other services. Those buy different capabilities. BotBar can use external channels when needed while keeping internal collaboration on its own digital path.

rows.label: Margin discipline
rows.detail: Measure hosting, storage, model use, voice, optional telephony and customer support; price paid services against their actual costs.

rows.label: Positioning
rows.detail: Compete on integrated team work and efficient coordination. No unmeasured speed, reliability or fully loaded cost ranking is claimed.

slides.sourceLabel: Transport can cost fractions of a cent. Full BotBar unit costs and margins still require production measurement.

slides.title:
ONE NETWORK.
MULTIPLE REVENUES.
slides.body: Earn from useful work, creator transactions and relevant distribution.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Each revenue stream has a customer and a reason to pay.
bullets: Team subscriptions, usage and white-label services.
A platform share of creator bot and app sales.
Promoted store listings and sponsored keyboard keys.

expanded.title: Each revenue stream has a customer and a reason to pay
body: Businesses pay for ongoing coordination and supported services. Creators earn by selling bots and apps; the platform earns its agreed share of those transactions. Suppliers pay for visible, relevant access to users.

The free keyboard and accessible network entry support distribution. Paid services, store economics and placements can monetize adoption without requiring every user to purchase the same subscription.

rows.label: Business teams
rows.detail: Recurring workspace and workflow services, plus usage where costs vary.

rows.label: Creators
rows.detail: Sell useful bots or apps and retain their agreed proceeds; BotBar earns the platform share.

rows.label: Advertisers and partners
rows.detail: Pay for clearly identified store promotion, keys and eligible referrals.

rows.label: Organizations
rows.detail: License white-label services and supported business offerings.

slides.sourceLabel: Revenue model. Pricing and commercial terms will be set through launch and customer agreements.

slides.title:
DISCOVERY,
IN THE WORKFLOW.
slides.body: Find a useful bot, add it to a team and reach it again where work happens.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Connect the point of discovery to repeat use.
bullets: Creators build and sell.
The store makes their bots discoverable.
Keyboard placement puts services within reach.

expanded.title: Connect the point of discovery to repeat use
body: A store listing alone does not create a habit. A useful bot can move from discovery into a customer’s team, contact list and keyboard, giving the creator a path to repeat adoption.

BotBar operates both the marketplace and a daily interaction surface. That creates distinct opportunities for transaction revenue, promotion and partner placement, while the user keeps control of their work.

rows.label: Placement value
rows.detail: Relevant exposure close to a user’s intended action.

rows.label: Creator value
rows.detail: Distribution, identity and a route to paying customers.

rows.label: User value
rows.detail: A way to find useful bots and return to the ones that help.

slides.sourceLabel: Paid placements are identified. Placement does not grant access to private data.

slides.title:
SHOW THE WORK.
EARN THE CUSTOMER.
slides.body: Start with one valuable workflow, then expand through teams, creators and partners.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Make the sales motion repeatable before widening it.
bullets: Demonstrate with service and outreach teams.
Convert useful pilots into recurring customers.
Grow through agencies, referrals and distribution.

expanded.title: Make the sales motion repeatable before widening it
body: Founder-led demonstrations establish the first business use cases. A launch team then turns them into onboarding, support, case studies and repeatable offers for similar customers.
The product can help create demonstrations and marketing materials. Dedicated marketing budget funds customer acquisition, while agency and white-label relationships extend distribution.

rows.label: Initial offer
rows.detail: A focused, supported workflow for follow-up or customer coordination.

rows.label: Expansion
rows.detail: More colleagues, connected bot teams and useful recurring tasks.

rows.label: Commercial measures
rows.detail: Paid activation, repeat use, retention, acquisition cost and support effort—not just signups.

slides.title:
AN ADDRESS.
A RELATIONSHIP.
A NETWORK.
slides.body: Durable handles connect people to bot teams, services and a marketplace they can return to.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Operate the network where identity becomes useful.
bullets: Owners build a recognizable bot identity.
Trusted contacts make collaboration easier to repeat.
Creators and users give each other reasons to join.

expanded.title: Operate the network where identity becomes useful
body: The domain-name era showed the value of an address people can remember. BotBar applies that intuition to bot relationships: a handle becomes useful when it reaches the right team and preserves the owner’s control.

The opportunity comes from operating the directory, vetting and store together with everyday work surfaces. Identity alone is not defensibility; useful connections, customer trust, repeat activity and creator participation must earn it.

rows.label: Retention
rows.detail: Contacts, trusted teams and recurring work encourage return visits.

rows.label: Distribution
rows.detail: Creators bring services; customers bring collaborators and demand.

rows.label: Operator role
rows.detail: Maintain the directory, admission standards and marketplace experience.

slides.title:
DEVELOPED
FOUNDATIONS.
A FOCUSED LAUNCH.
slides.body: Founder-led development has demonstrated core connections. The next step is a reliable customer experience.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Turn demonstrated connections into independent customer use.
bullets: Bot messaging, file exchange and shared voice demonstrations.
Complete the connected workspace and repeatable onboarding.
Expand supported business and meeting workflows.

expanded.title: Turn demonstrated connections into independent customer use
body: Early supervised demonstrations include bot-to-bot messages, a small file exchange and a shared human-and-assistant voice conversation. They establish foundations; customer readiness requires the complete ordinary-user workflow.
The launch path brings accounts, handles, contacts, permissions, tools and the visual workspace together. Zoom, Teams, creator commerce and additional devices remain part of the product direction.

rows.label: Launch readiness
rows.detail: A customer can enroll, connect a team, complete useful work and return to the result.

rows.label: Operating readiness
rows.detail: The team can onboard customers, handle issues, measure service costs and maintain reliable delivery.

slides.sourceLabel: Development demonstrations are not a claim that every illustrated workflow or integration is already available.

slides.title:
FUND THE LAUNCH.
BUILD THE TEAM.
slides.body: Turn founder-led development into an operating business ready to acquire and serve customers.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Capital for the organization around the product.
bullets: People to operate and maintain the service.
Marketing and partnerships to sell it.
Onboarding and customer support for launch demand.

expanded.title: Capital for the organization around the product
body: The request is for investment in a capable operating team, a marketing budget and the customer-service capacity to support a fast launch. Development has a foundation; the business needs people who can run it, bring in customers and keep them successful.

Funding should connect to concrete launch outcomes: a supported customer experience, repeatable acquisition, responsive service and clear operating economics. Raise size, hiring sequence and detailed budget are part of the investment discussion.

rows.label: Operations + product continuity
rows.detail: Service operations, release quality, reliability and ongoing product support.

rows.label: Marketing + distribution
rows.detail: Demonstrations, campaigns, partnerships, sales and repeatable onboarding materials.

rows.label: Customer success
rows.detail: Hands-on onboarding, responsive help and capacity that grows with demand.
